text: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the November 5th, 2026 monthly audit committee meeting. I am the chair of this committee. I'm Anne Donahue, the at-large member of the Loudoun County School Board. With me are fellow committee members, Mr. Jonathan Pepper from the Dulles District and Ms. Amy Ricardi from the Sterling District. As a reminder, this meeting is being audio-recorded only, not video-recorded and not live-streamed, but the audio recording will be available for the public to listen to in the future through the LCPS website.

Now that we have done our call to order, the second item on our agenda is public comment. Is there anyone for public comment tonight? Seeing none, we will move right on to agenda item number three, approval of the minutes from the September 10th, 2026 audit committee meeting, which was the last monthly meeting of this committee. The draft minutes are in the packet and have also been posted on BoardDocs for review. If my colleagues have any suggestions for

edits or corrections, now is the time to speak up, and if there are no corrections or amendments or adjustments, I will entertain a motion to accept the minutes. Ms. Ricardi? Oh. Was that your hand? No. Yeah. Okay. Mr. Pepper. I move to approve the minutes of the September 10, 2026 audit committee meeting. Second. Thank you. That motion has been properly made by Mr. Pepper and seconded by Ms. Ricardi. Is there any discussion?

Seeing none, all those in favor, please say aye. Aye. Aye. Aye. That motion passes unanimously with all three committee members present and in support. And now we will move on to the first of our information items, item 4.01, the quarterly status update for July through September, presented by our esteemed auditor general, Mr. Woods. The floor is yours. Thank you. Good evening, Madam Chair and members of the audit committee.

This evening, I will provide a brief quarterly update regarding the activities of the Office of the Auditor General, covering the period from July 2026 through September 2026. Next slide, please. Tonight's agenda will cover audit activities during the quarter, the status of current and upcoming audits, quality assurance and improvement program activities, which I'll reference

as QAIP going forward, training and professional development, hotline activity, and any committee action items regarding this quarterly update. The next several slides summarize the office's activities during the reporting period and highlight both completed work and ongoing activities. Next slide. During the quarter, the office completed the transportation management audit,

which is being presented separately to the committee this evening. The office currently has four engagements in process. Teacher Extended Jefferson Contracts, which we are in the reporting phase; Register Information Management and Data Integrity, which is in the early stages of the reporting phase; Comprehensive Staffing and Process Efficiency, which is currently in the fieldwork phase;

and the LCPS and Police Department's Information Sharing Protocols. That one is in the early planning phase for this one. Work continues on these engagements, and the committee will receive updates as milestones are reached and reports are completed. All right. Go back please. Yeah.

All right. Upcoming audits. Looking ahead, the office has identified two upcoming audits. The first will be Employee Reporting Mechanisms and Retaliation Complaint Oversight. This audit will examine the process used to receive, evaluate, and respond to employee concerns and allegations of retaliation. The second is the Federal Grant Compliance. This audit will assess whether federal grant programs are being administered in

accordance with applicable requirements and whether supporting documentation is sufficient to withstand external review. Quality assurance remains a key focus area for the office. During the quarter, the office finalized revisions to the audit manual, the internal OAG's manual, which we use to conduct our audits and perform our work,

developed an AI prompt library to help facilitate the efficiency of audits and consistency, and conducted internal quality reviews. The office will continue office process improvements through the development of quality review checklists, enhancement of internal control assessment tools, and ongoing refinements to audit methodologies. Looking ahead, the office plans to conduct its November QAIP

meeting in the upcoming weeks. This will incorporate lessons learned from recently completed audits, completed or continued targeted auditor training, and further prepare for future external quality assessment requirements. I am also pleased to report that no significant impairments to independence were identified during the reporting period.

The office continues to invest in professional development to strengthen audit examination capabilities. During the quarter, staff earned 40 continuing professional education credits through participation in the Association of Certified Fraud Examiners Global Fraud Conference. Additional continuing or CPE credits were also earned through the ACFE Certified Fraud Examiner review course. Additional training has been identified through the Institute of Internal Auditors,

and is planned later this year in December. That training will specifically focus on auditing internal controls related to cybersecurity as we prepare for upcoming audits. During the reporting period, the office received two hotline submissions. Each submission was reviewed and evaluated in accordance with established procedures. The hotline continues to serve as an important reporting mechanism that supports

accountability and transparency. Next slide. At this time, there are no committee action items associated with this quarterly update. All committee-related matters for the current reporting cycle remain current and in compliance. This concludes OAG's quarterly status update. I am happy to answer any questions the committee may have.

For clarity of the record on something, and Mr. Pepper had an issue come up and had to step out. Ms. Riccardi, do you have questions? Go ahead. Yes. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you so much for the presentation. I just had a couple quick questions just to make sure that I'm level setting, because I know we didn't have a meeting last month. So I just want to make sure I didn't miss anything. So did we have a cybersecurity task on the list of items

for our upcoming audit? And if we did, did I miss it in here? So it wasn't in this particular status update, but for the approved audit plan, the committee did approve the cybersecurity audit. We have training early December, and so planning of that audit will probably start January. We want to start somewhere in December, but given the

fact that we have training and the holidays, that audit will probably start in January. And so it wasn't included in these upcoming ones since initially this status update was for that period through September. And so the future quarterly updates will have that audit in it. Okay. I just wanted to make sure I didn't miss something in all of that, so I appreciate that update. Mm-hmm. And then,

as far as bandwidth for additional audits in the future, have you had a chance to look at the plan, or were you just still trying to schedule the existing stuff and we'll figure out if you've got bandwidth for more at a later time? And I'm not trying to put more on your plate, I'm just asking. I think we had a conversation again. I'm just trying to make sure I understood that we had a conversation about maybe potential bandwidth at some point in time. Correct. We did.

We thought about coming back, discussing do we want to add other audits to the plan. And then I think it was determined that November might be a little too soon to add those audits. But I do think that's a continuing conversation that we can have at the beginning of the year. Right now, I think we have enough or adequate work for the office. And so I think right now we're in a good place, but we will definitely continue to have this conversation, and we can also revisit that conversation in December.

Okay, great. Thanks so much. I appreciate that. Thank you, Mr. Woods. I don't have any questions right now about your update, so we'll move on to item number 40.02, overview of audit report, transportation management system. Back to you, Mr. Woods. Thank you. Next up, I will provide an overview of the results of the audit of transportation

management. The presentation summarizes the audit objectives, overall conclusions, key findings, management responses, and the OAG's assessment. Next slide, please. Tonight, I will begin with our risk classification methodology, followed by the audit objectives, and background information regarding transportation services. I will then discuss the overall audit opinion, summarize the

key findings, review management's corrective action plans, and conclude with the OAG's assessment. Before discussing the results, I would like to briefly explain our risk classification methodology. Findings are classified as high, moderate, or low based on the significance of the condition, the potential impact to the organization, and the urgency of management attention required.

In this audit, we identified one high-risk finding and three findings classified as moderate or low risk. The objective of this audit was to evaluate the effectiveness of transportation management controls and determine whether transportation operations are managed and monitored in accordance with LCPS policies, applicable federal and state regulations, and industry leading practices.

Transportation supports over 77,000 students, operates over 750 buses, manages more than 500 daily routes, and facilitates approximately eight million miles of travel annually. Given the scale and importance of these operations, effective controls and oversight are critical to ensuring efficient service delivery and student safety.

The first finding classified as... Oh, did I skip that? Sorry. Yeah. Based on the audit procedures performed, the office concluded that transportation controls should be enhanced. While transportation services has established processes and a strong operational foundation, we identified opportunities to strengthen data integrity, internal communication, performance monitoring, and operational oversight. Overall, the audit resulted in one high-risk finding, as previously mentioned, and

three moderate or low-risk findings. The first finding, classified as high risk, involved incomplete and unreliable operational data. We identified missing pre- and post-trip inspection reports, missing driver login and logout information, and limited availability of historical transportation data. These issues reduce accountability and weaken oversight.

They also hinder management's ability to effectively monitor performance and compliance. The second finding on the right, classified as moderate risk, involved communication coordination gaps among dispatch personnel, drivers, routing staff, supervisors, and school administrators. These communication challenges can contribute to service disruptions, delays, unmet transportation needs, and limited awareness of

important student accommodations and behavioral concerns. The third finding, also classified as moderate risk, involved the absence of a formal performance monitoring framework. We found that transportation services had not established documented key performance indicators, performance targets, or a comprehensive performance reporting process. As a result, management has a limited ability to measure effectiveness and identify

operational trends. The fourth finding on the right, classified as low risk, involved weaknesses in monitoring vehicle idling. We identified instances where buses exceeded the established limit and determined that monitoring and enforcement practices could be improved. The impact includes increased fuel consumption, vehicle wear, emissions, and potential compliance concerns. Next slide.

To address the identified issues, the office recommended strengthening transportation data controls and record retention practices, improving communication and coordination among stakeholders, developing a formal performance monitoring framework, and enhancing oversight of vehicle idling requirements. Management agreed to all the findings and recommendations. Their planned corrective actions include enhanced data retention and reporting capabilities, standardized communication procedures, development of key performance

indicators, routine performance reviews, strengthening idling compliance monitoring, and additional staff training and accountability measures. Overall, the office found that transportation services has a strong foundation supported by established safety practices, operational experience, and technology resources. The findings identified in this audit represent opportunities to further strengthen

oversight, data reliability, communication, and performance processes. The Office of Auditor General highly appreciates and commends transportation's cooperation throughout the engagement and their commitment to implementing corrective actions. Once fully implemented, these improvements should enhance operational effectiveness, accountability, student safety across transportation services. Next slide.

This concludes the presentation of the audit of transportation management. I am happy to answer any questions from the committee. Would you like to start, Ms. McCarty? No, I don't mind. I've got some questions, so. All right. Thank you, Mr. Woods. So,

having reviewed the audit report, which is also on BoardDocs and in our packet, which includes the response of Mr. Memon from the administration, who is here with us this evening. Thank you for being here. It looks like by and large, the administration concurs with the findings in this audit report. Is that your understanding, Mr. Woods? Yes.

Okay. That's my read as well. In particular, regarding your first finding and recommendation, the one that you've categorized as high risk, and I understand that the administration disagrees with that categorization. We've had other conversations about choice of language generally with regard to assessment of risk criteria. But what I wanted to ask you, Mr. Woods, was in

the administration's response on that issue, Mr. Memon states that they have already taken some corrective actions. And so I wondered a couple of things, I suppose, which is firstly, when you put out these audit reports and make recommendations, if the administration

says, "We are following up, we are making changes," do you do any kind of after action to verify, check on the corrective actions that the administration says that they're taking? And do you- Given the stated corrective actions that the administration put forward in their management response, do you feel comfortable that their corrective

actions address, in particular, the first finding regarding incomplete and unreliable operational data? I would say their response addresses the finding and the recommendation, and it is adequate. And it is well-written and put-together, and it has target dates. We have not followed up

with their corrective action items. But during the audit, transportation was very responsive and very open, answered all the questions, gave us access to all their solutions, i.e., software. And so I'm very confident that those corrective actions will be taken.

But we do follow up. It is part of the audit process. It follows up after the audit is done, and then we give them time to complete their audit or their corrective actions, and then we do follow up. Sometimes those follow-ups can be an email. Sometimes we can go to their webpage and see things being updated. In this particular instance, we do have-- Well, I don't know if we still currently have access to some of the solutions, but if we do, we may be able to just go into the solutions and just see and do

a few checks to determine if they've been updated. But because they are pretty extensive on their corrective actions, this will be a follow-up through an email or a meeting. But we have not done that yet. Understandably, since this was a very recent audit report. That's helpful. Thank you. And just to be clear, when I'm asking about follow-up, it is not to suggest in any way that we don't

trust that management and that the administration is going to follow through with the steps they've indicated they're going to take. But since that is my understanding of your purpose as an auditor and our purpose as board members, our role is to oversee what is happening with LCPS administration to make sure that we are fulfilling our due diligence and you're fulfilling your due diligence. Don't want to have any questions. And might I ask, I think one of the corrective actions on the first finding

was a vendor issue. The vendor was keeping data for 12 months and purging that data. And so it becomes a contract issue to tell the vendor, "We would like to keep this data longer. We have different retention requirements." And so that is reaching out to the vendor and ensuring we keep that data for longer than 12 months. And so that one, I believe, is something they've already worked on.

Okay. Thank you for that. I have a couple of questions about some of the specifics in the audit report and response. And I hate to put Mr. Mahmoud on the spot, but I am wondering if he will be in a better position to know the answers to some of the questions that I have. So I'll start throwing a few out there, Mr. Woods, and if you don't know, then I may encourage Mr. Mahmoud to come up to a microphone and chime in if you feel comfortable doing so.

Yeah. Phone a friend. Thank you, Mr. Mahmoud, for being here and for agreeing to be put on the spot. And can you introduce your phone-a-friend resource? Yeah, this is Mr. Scott Davies, our Director of Transportation. Thank you, Mr. Davies. Even better. So I had a couple of questions about

some of the things that were mentioned in the article, and in particular, this discussion of the idling vehicles. When we're talking in here about the idling of the vehicles, is this idling for weather reasons or traffic reasons, or because we've dropped off one load of kids and we're waiting for something else to happen, or some combination of all of the above? Some combination of all of the above, but the latter is the majority of the idling. Drivers are waiting.

It's either hot outside or it's cold outside, and they're running the air conditioner or the heater to stay warm or stay comfortable. And we are working on that because it's using fuel, which is an expensive resource at this particular moment, but it's always an expensive resource, and we want to conserve as much as we can. So we are constantly counseling drivers to conserve fuel to be efficient. If they're cold or they're hot, they can go inside the building at the schools where they're waiting. And so we are addressing that.

Okay. And my understanding of part of the concern with the audit findings was a lack of consistent pre- and post-trip inspections, and sometimes missing driver log entries. Curious, do the drivers-- Obviously they're trained, and they're trained that this is part of the requirements of their job. But

what are they told as to why these are part of the requirements of the job? So the logging in and out, that is how their time is kept. The first thing they do when they arrive at the bus in the morning is log in, and that's how they clock in and how their compensation starts. And at the end of their morning run, they generally clock out. And then do the same in the afternoon. The pre-trip inspection is the majority of their training time

when they get their CDL with us is the pre-trip inspection. That is a very critical, mandated, legally required If the tablet is not working, because right now we do it via tablet and it's done electronically. They scan various sections of the bus as they inspect them. So you get real-time information. You get real-time information. Sometimes those tablets aren't working. They have paper backups. But

some drivers, especially those who have been around for a while, they're not always-- Complacency is one of our enemies, and so we have to constantly remind and police that to make sure that they're not getting complacent on that requirement. Thank you. Thank you for that. As best as you can tell, do you train them that it is a critical safety issue as opposed to just a job requirement, license

requirement? Yes. No, we train them, because that's how you find out if the oil's leaking, or you have no coolant, or if there's something that was messed with overnight through vandalism or something of that nature. Okay. Well, that might be all I have for right now. I'm going to look at my notes. Go ahead, Ms. Ricardi. Thank you, Madam Chair. Well, thank you so much. And

this is, I think, one of the first-- I think we have one report that we got earlier in the spring, but this is, I think, the first full cycle report that we've had. So I'm a big picture down to the details person, so I think the first thing I have a question about is just how this process went. And as we're doing these debriefs, I think it's really helpful to hear from both sides of the

report and to make sure that we give you all plenty of time to respond, too. So I wanted just to say, and I appreciate the feedback that the team was really responsive and gave you access to the data that you needed to be able to do what you did. I think my first question is just about the population size of the study and what that looked like. So did we use a big enough sample size, and is that mandated through the OAG process, or what does that look like?

So I'll just walk you through the audit. We perform site visits, so we visited their main hub, which is off Sicklin Road. We also went to the western hub, which is in Leesburg or Purcellville. And so we walked through the facilities. We got to see this dispatch. We got to see where the nuts and bolts are. We got to see where the extra

parts are kept. We walked in and saw all the buses, where they wash buses, and explained to us that sometimes they can freeze in the winter. We got to meet the mechanics. We talked to mechanics. We saw reports where they would sign their inspections and their license. We interviewed drivers, and one of the things we learned interviewing drivers is if you have your CDL, you have to know all the parts of the bus or the truck. And why that matters is they have the knowledge and the expertise

when they're doing their post and pre-trip. And so the data may not be in there, but they are fully aware and have the expertise to know the parts on their bus. And that is done even outside of here, just through having that CDL. And so we learned that doing the interviews with the bus drivers. We got to see where they can actually, in real-time, monitor buses at that hub off of Sickling, where

they have live feeds, I believe, on some of the buses, not all the buses, where they can see and monitor how buses are driving. We got to see where the communications area is, where if a family has a concern if the bus is late and they call in, we got to see that center. We got to see training facilities where they keep their training folders on buses. And so we got to see a lot of the transportation

services division. It is very robust, it's very complex, and they do a very good job of busing our kids every day. There were some things we did identify in the audit, but those were, even though you might see a high risk, we didn't find any instances of bus drivers driving who had violated the law. We didn't find any bus drivers who didn't have their CDLs or expired

CDLs. And so the audit is reporting on just what we found. The audit is never going to fully identify all the good things they do, and we try to capture that in the executive summary of the audit. But it is a very complex situation or process that they run. And they do a very good job at it. And so we did all that, and these were the items of the audit that we found.

In the criteria section, and just to go back to the idling part, if you're wondering where that came from, the Pupil Transportation Handbook, it does require that there's zero idling. But as Mr. Davies pointed out, there are instances where it is cold outside, and you may not want the students to enter a cold or hot bus. And so I think those are things we can work on.

But that particular finding, for that reason, is assessed at a lower risk. But we do want to be cognizant of our fuel consumption and our emissions. So, I hope that answers your question. Yeah. I guess what I was really going to the population size of the buses that you looked at. And by the way, we got to see the operations and orientation for the school board, which is fascinating to me. There's so much going on with transportation, and I know we do a really great job of getting our students to school safely,

and back home safely as well. But I want to make sure, number one, from a data perspective, that you had a big enough data set in order to come up with the findings. Now, for sampling purposes, when we reviewed particular buses for maintenance records, for post and pre-trip, for idling, that was a sample. And so also with the interviews with the drivers, that was also a sample. Other areas, because we were given access to

their software, we were able to look at- Okay ... the entire population size for a given scope period. But for reviewing buses, for idling, for reviewing pre-trips and post-trips, for interviewing staff, those were samples. Great. Thank you for that. And then, Mr. Mahmoud, I know you got dropped into this, I think probably in the middle or towards the end, I would assume, of the audit. Is that right? I just want to make...

Yeah. So, obviously, Mr. Woods reached out to me, I think even before I actually officially started. Yeah. And looped me in, so I definitely appreciate that. So as he mentioned already that there was sufficient timing given. So yes, I did get looped into towards the end of the audit process, but I was looped in very early. Like as soon as I was available to be looped in. I think Mr. Woods did a fantastic job of keeping me updated and sending me a

copy of the preliminary report, I believe in mid-August, and I started in late August. So, that was very timely in that regard. So you all had already done the study by the time you came on board, and you were just working on the report at that point? Yes. Okay. And given that we knew about the transition- Right ... we knew about the incoming new COO, we opted just to wait. And so, the three

individuals who were available, which was the acting COO, the transportation, Scott Davies, and Mahmoud. We waited till Mahmoud had an email address, and then we forwarded the information to them, and so he can be in the loop. And so going forward, he'll be responsible for this area, along with Mr. Davies.

And I believe it was Don Traynor who was also included on that distribution. Great. And then from the report perspective, do you feel like you've gotten some really helpful and useful information as you're getting started in this role and moving forward to help refine, I guess, operations and best practices for the department? Yeah, absolutely. And I think definitely, that was very helpful coming in, understanding obviously, we

acknowledge the report, the work that was done behind it. But having that coming in, obviously gives us something to make sure that we're measuring as we are going forward. So that, definitely in that regard, definitely very helpful. Great. And then as far as the KPIs go, because I'm very familiar with building out KPIs, is that a best practice within LCPS? I mean, do we do KPIs? I don't know. I haven't seen

sets of KPIs at this point. So, I see that that was a recommendation, but just in the goal-setting process, are we using that model across either department and/or LCPS as a whole? For transportation, we have specific, we don't usually call them KPIs, but we have performance goals that we establish for ourselves in terms of morning and afternoon on-time performance, as well as fleet readiness. Those are our key ones. And then also responsiveness for parent

concerns that are submitted and discipline issues that arise on buses, and response time for meeting our drivers' needs. Right. And is the on-time performance, how are we doing with that? I believe right now we're generally in the 90s, upper 90s for morning, and in the afternoon, we're in the mid to upper 80s, percentage-wise. And the reason we have the afternoon

is so much lower than that morning is we don't have control over when the buses start. Sure. We have to wait for the schools to release us. Yeah. That's always hard to have a metric when you don't have control of all the inputs to the metric. Yeah, absolutely. I get it. All right. Well, thank you. Is there anything else you wanted to add that would be helpful to us as we're reading through this and evaluating it? Well, first of all, I want to give credit to my entire team. From our drivers and attendants to our mechanics and the supervisors that

run the show every single day and make it work, they get all the credit for the wonderful work that gets done there. And I have another question just for another time, but just to put this out there, too. One of the things, we just heard in the previous committee meeting that we're at a really high percentage of staffing. We're at like 99.4, I think it was, percentage of a fill rate, right, of staff. So, I don't know that our bus drivers are at that same number. Right.

So, I'm keeping in mind what we need to do to continue to incent people to apply and become bus drivers. I've seen the ads. They've popped up on my social media, so I know we're putting ads out there. But one thing I would like, and as offline from this conversation, is I'd love to hear from you all about what you think we can do to help incent more individuals that are interested in becoming bus drivers, and how we can really get that pipeline filled, too. Because I'd love to see that at the 99.4% fill

rate moving forward. And as we're getting into the budget season, I think that's going to be really helpful for us, too. One thing we are trying to do right now is shorten the time span from the time someone demonstrates interest in becoming a driver, to the time they're in the seat behind the wheel. That has historically been stretched over many months, because it takes a few months to get in the door, and then once you're in the door, it takes a couple of months to get trained. We are trying to squeeze that down as much as we can, so that people can start earning a paycheck as quickly as possible when they raise

their hand. Thank you for that. If anything else comes up, I would really love to hear from you. Did you want to add to that? No, I was just going to add to what Mr. Davies already said. So coming from a different jurisdiction, I'm going to add on to what Mr. Davies already said, that I do believe our team does a fantastic job. Obviously, transportation is extremely complex. We don't deliver Amazon packages, we deliver kids, right? So it's not as simple as just putting it into a software and churning out numbers

and say, "This is how we're doing it." But I think the team does an amazing job. The other thing I have to add, and Mr. Davies already touched on that, is our training piece is crucial, and I do believe that I am seeing, while we do have vacancies, I'm seeing a less number here than I'm used to seeing because of the fact that our teams are constantly doing that work and also training more and more of our drivers.

Thank you. Just following up on some things that Ms. Ricardi said, I was wondering, while going through all of this paperwork, wondering how much our drivers generally feel like they are valued members of the educational team. And this similar, maybe is not a conversation for this venue right here right now, but, I do wonder if that has an impact on when you were saying earlier that there may be

some drivers who are not doing all of their appropriate checks every day. And if that is the case, could that be tied into if they feel like they're valued members of the educational team? And those are some questions I had about how much are the drivers getting trained on our PBIS, and how to deal with IEPs and special needs kids and all of those kind of things, which again, is only tangentially related, I think, to the audit

question, and is going to be more appropriate for an offline conversation, possibly with your team, possibly with HRTD. Mm-hmm. But is also something that I want to follow up on, because like Ms. Ricardi, I would also like to see our numbers go up for our fill rates of our drivers. But that being said, I have a seventh grader and a fourth grader in LCPS. We've been using LCPS Transportation for a long time. And

I've been very happy as a parent and as a board member with how the transportation works, and am very impressed with Mr. Mamoon's team and Mr. Davies' team, because it is very complex and I've not been involved in this level at any other school district since I was a student myself. But, knowing how Loudoun is geographically very large and very diverse as far as the state of the roads in different parts of the county and the density of neighborhoods in different parts

of the county, it's a tall order to get our 80,000 students to our 100 schools. And I'm very appreciative for all of the team that makes that happen. And also appreciative for your cooperation with Mr. Woods, and that Mr. Woods was able to work so easily with your team. I think that speaks well of everyone involved in this process, and I

like what we're doing here, where we have representatives from the group being audited can also be here to answer our questions. So I don't have any other questions. If you don't have any other questions right now, then I think we can move on to our third information item, 4.03, Revised Policy 3410, Office of the Auditor General. Back to you again, Mr. Woods. Thank you.

The next item before committee is review of proposed revisions to Policy 3410, Office of the Auditor General. As reflected in the agenda materials, the purpose of these revisions is not to make substantive changes to the authority, mission, or professional responsibilities of the OAG. Rather, the proposed updates are primarily intended to improve alignment between Policy 3410 and Policy 2310, Committees of the School Board, following revisions that were previously

adopted to Policy 2310. The proposed changes clarify the audit committee's oversight responsibility, reinforce the distinction between oversight and direct participation in audit activities, and improve consistency regarding governance, reporting relationships, authority, and responsibilities already established within existing school board policy. The revisions also incorporate updates to terminology and professional standards referenced to better reflect

current internal auditing guidance and practices. Tonight's discussion is intended to obtain committee feedback on the proposed revisions. No action is required from the committee at this time. Staff will incorporate any feedback received this evening and return a final version of this policy as a future action item for the committee's consideration. With that, I will provide a brief overview of the proposed revisions

and answer any questions the committee may have. So the first red line updates were to line six, just for terminology or clarity. Very small, going to the professionalism. So in B, we updated this area because during the process, we noted that when we first adopted Policy 3410 The Institute of Internal Auditors

labeled their standards something different, and they updated their terminology. So we just were updating the terminology to align to the exact language they now use. They went from international standards to global internal audit standards. So it was updating that terminology to better reflect IIA's terminology that they use now. Moving down, we also updated areas where there's more

clarity to identify who we are referring to, so superintendent and cabinet as opposed to senior leadership, which could be a little bit more broad. And so we want to narrow the scope in that language. Moving on, just more clerical or clarifications in our policy. I want to jump down to... Well,

next page or scroll down a little bit to... Oh, sorry. Page two. Yeah, just a little bit higher. Oh, a little bit. Right there. I want to just highlight overview for the authority overview.
